headline: Rhode Island governor race enters final month with a stark campaign-cash divide
dek: New filings show independent Ken Block with $263,000 on hand, Democrat Helena Foulkes with $214,000 and Republican Aaron Guckian with just over $7,000 as early voting approaches.
body: Rhode Island’s three major candidates for governor are entering the final month of the general-election campaign with sharply different financial positions. Reports due Tuesday to the [Rhode Island Board of Elections](https://elections.ri.gov/campaign-finance/public-info) show independent Ken Block with the most cash available for the closing stretch, Democrat Helena Foulkes close behind and Republican Aaron Guckian operating with a much smaller reserve. The figures offer a measurable look at the resources each campaign can use before voters begin casting ballots.

According to [WPRI’s review of the filings](https://www.aol.com/articles/block-leads-foulkes-campaign-cash-034332000.html), Block reported about $263,000 in his account as of Monday. That total included $190,000 in personal loans he made to his campaign during September. His report covered July 1 through Oct. 5, during which he raised $63,000 and spent $80,000. The personal-loan figure is important context: cash on hand describes what a campaign can spend, but it does not mean all of that money came from outside donors.

Foulkes reported $214,000 on hand. Her filing covered the shorter period from Sept. 2 through Oct. 5, after she won the Democratic primary against Gov. Dan McKee. WPRI reported that she raised $381,000 and spent $545,000 during that period, while her campaign has spent more than $5 million this year. The new balance suggests a campaign that has had access to substantial support but also has been spending heavily as it moved from a competitive primary into the general election.

Guckian, the Republican nominee, reported a little more than $7,000 on hand after raising roughly that amount and spending about $12,000 during the same Sept. 2-to-Oct. 5 period, WPRI reported. That leaves him with considerably less money for advertising, field organizing and voter contact than either of his two major opponents. The filing does not determine the election’s outcome, but it narrows the amount of paid communication his campaign can deploy without a major new infusion of money.

The party accounts widen the gap. WPRI reported that the Rhode Island Democratic Party had about $314,000 in its state account, compared with roughly $22,000 for the Republican Party. The Democratic Governors Association also put $500,000 into an affiliated Rhode Island group supporting Foulkes, according to a Board of Elections filing cited in the report. Those party and outside resources are separate from the candidates’ own balances, but they can still affect the volume and reach of campaign activity voters see.

The financial reports arrive as the race is also being shaped by the question of whether Guckian should remain in the contest. [The Boston Globe reported](https://bostonglobe-prod.cdn.arcpublishing.com/2026/10/06/metro/rhode-island-governor-race-foulkes-guckian-block-election/) that Block and some of his supporters have pressed Guckian to leave, arguing that Block would have a stronger chance against Foulkes in a two-way race. Guckian has said he will stay in the race, and the Globe noted that it is already too late to remove his name from the ballot. That dispute makes the cash figures part of a broader argument about whether the November contest is effectively three-sided or could become a one-on-one race.

Foulkes won the Sept. 9 Democratic primary over McKee by 62% to 38%, according to WPRI’s account, and the report said she won all 39 cities and towns. Since then, Democratic leaders and organized labor have begun consolidating behind her, while Block has tried to position himself as the principal alternative. The candidates’ fundraising reports cannot measure enthusiasm, volunteer strength or issue preferences, but they do show how much financial capacity each campaign brings into the period when many voters will first focus on the race.

Early voting begins Oct. 14, and the general election is Nov. 3. The three candidates are scheduled to take part in a televised debate on Oct. 20 from Rhode Island College, according to WPRI. Between now and then, campaigns will be competing for attention across television, digital media, mail and local organizing. The next meaningful test will be whether Block can turn his cash advantage into broader support, whether Foulkes can maintain her lead while rebuilding her account, and whether Guckian can raise enough to remain visible through Election Day.
author: NorthEast News Desk
